verdicts.why: A technical music term for the melodic subject of a piece; it names a structural element and takes no attitude toward it.
Names the courtesy formula itself (best wishes); the word labels a kind act of speech without judging the person it is sent to.
The scientific sense for how a machine or substance acts under given conditions is purely descriptive, with no approval or contempt in it.
A theological label for one of the three named virtues; the referent is prized, but the word simply names it rather than praising.
The sign reads 'closed' merely reports wording; there is no attitude toward the text or its author.
Interpreting or conveying an impression is a neutral act; the judgement lies in what is read, not in the verb.
Making sense of written language is the plain core sense, as neutral as 'see' or 'hear'.
To read law or history at university is a plain (mainly British) term for studying a subject, with no attitude attached.
A gauge that reads forty degrees is reporting a value; no judgement of the instrument or the reading is carried.
'Do you read me?' is radio-register but attitude-free; it asks about reception, not about the hearer.
Retrieving data from a storage medium is a computing term with no evaluative charge.
Reading for a part names a routine step in casting; it neither flatters nor belittles the actor.
Becoming linked or united is plain description, as the sentences about joining a party or a regiment show.
Coming together or making contact is neutral; nothing in the word approves or dismisses the things joined.
Calling someone 'a power' in a field states that they hold influence; any awe comes from the fact, not from the word.
Physical strength named plainly; a strong meaning, not an attitude.
Electrical energy is a technical referent with no evaluative load.
'A world power' is the standard descriptive term in politics for an influential state, used without praise or blame.
The physics quantity measured in watts is definitional and carries no attitude.
The mathematical exponent sense is pure notation with nothing to judge.
Unlike its neighbours 'tycoon' and 'mogul', 'power' for a big businessperson only states their reach, not admiration or resentment.
In 'pomp and circumstance' the word names ceremonial display itself; any grandeur is the referent's, not a stance the word takes.
Being short of money or time states a deficit as a fact; the shortfall is a bad referent, but the word does not scold.
A short memory is a plain measure of poor retention; the reproach sometimes heard in the phrase comes from context, not from 'short' itself.
The phonetic sense for vowel or syllable duration is a technical classification with no attitude.
